passage: Rosa's coat was an old one, with the sleeves rolled twice. At the school gate in Hamburg, Oskar tugged a sleeve and laughed, "Did you get that from a museum?" Three boys giggled. Two girls looked away. Rosa pulled her hands inside the sleeves and said nothing, her ears burning. At recess she took the coat off and stood in the cold in her thin jumper, and Oskar blinked, as if this was not what he had wanted. Only Lena, near the fence, held out a scarf, and Rosa took it without a word.

qa.q: How were the sleeves of Rosa's coat arranged?
qa.a: The sleeves of Rosa's coat were rolled twice.

qa.q: What might Rosa feel when standing in the cold without the coat?
qa.a: Rosa feels ashamed and quietly resentful; taking the coat off shows a wish to make the difference vanish, even at the cost of warmth.

qa.q: What could a bystander or adult do when someone is laughed at for old clothes?
qa.a: A bystander or adult could stay beside the person, give a kind gesture as Lena did, or speak up calmly to say the joke is not funny.

qa.q: How might Lena see Rosa in that moment?
qa.a: Lena seems to have seen someone cold and hurt rather than someone funny, and chose one small kind act by offering the scarf.

grounding: A child in an old coat is laughed at, shrinks, and takes the coat off to hide the difference until one kind gesture arrives.

passage: In the school canteen Tarun opened his dented steel tiffin. Brown bread, with jam his mother had made. "Is that from a science lab?" said Lokesh, and Piyush snorted. Zoya kept eating, eyes down. Tarun closed the lid halfway. "It is nice," he said, too quietly. The duty teacher was scolding juniors at the far table. Tarun ate three bites in the shadow of the lid, then dropped the rest in the dustbin, and told himself he did not care about their faces. He walked out before the bell, and nobody noticed.

qa.q: What did Tarun's tiffin contain?
qa.a: Tarun's tiffin had brown bread with jam his mother had made.

qa.q: What does Tarun's dropping the bread in the dustbin suggest about how Tarun feels?
qa.a: Tarun feels embarrassed and a bit resentful; throwing the food away and telling himself he does not care hides how much the laughing stung.

qa.q: What could Tarun try before the next lunch break?
qa.a: Tarun could sit with someone kind, or tell the duty teacher what happened; one ally makes being different easier.

qa.q: What might Zoya be feeling while eating with eyes down?
qa.a: Zoya may feel uncomfortable and unwilling to join the laughing, but also afraid of becoming the next target.

grounding: A child with a homemade tiffin is laughed at and quietly copies the group by hiding the food, learning that difference has a price.

passage:
Monday. Neelam read the poem aloud and said “school” the way they said it back home in Muzaffarpur. Dhruv repeated it in a squeaky voice. The whole row laughed. Neelam finished the poem looking only at the page.
Thursday. She did not raise her hand once. At home she stood before the steel almirah mirror, saying “school, school, school” the way Dhruv's group did, until her mother asked who she was talking to.
The next Monday. Ms Kaur asked for a reader. Neelam kept her eyes down. When Dhruv read, badly, she said nothing, but pressed her pencil so hard the tip snapped.

qa.q: Where did Neelam practise saying the word at home?
qa.a: She practised in front of the steel almirah mirror.

qa.q: What might Neelam be feeling when her pencil tip snapped?
qa.a: She is likely resentful and hurt; she keeps silent while Dhruv reads badly, but her anger comes out through the pencil.

qa.q: How could Ms Kaur support Neelam after the first Monday?
qa.a: She could stop the mimicking straight away, tell the class accents are welcome, and quietly check in with Neelam so she feels safe to read again.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see what he did?
qa.a: Dhruv probably thought it was a harmless joke that made the row laugh, and has no idea Neelam now avoids reading.

grounding: Shows a child laughed at for her regional accent who shrinks, copies the group and quietly resents it over several days.

passage:
Come, Kiran, sit. You say they laughed at your old school bag? Let me tell you about my shorts. I am your Ajoba, Omkar, and in 1971 I had exactly one pair, patched at the back in a different blue.
On the first day of Class 5, a boy named Vasant pointed and shouted, “Map of India!” The whole class laughed, even my friend Datta. I sat on that patch all day and did not go to the board once, even when I knew the answer.
For weeks I walked home the long way, alone. Then one day Datta walked with me and said nothing about shorts. That walk mattered more than any new cloth.

qa.q: What did Vasant shout about the patch?
qa.a: He shouted, "Map of India!"

qa.q: How was young Omkar feeling on that first day?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and humiliated; he sat on the patch all day and didn't go to the board even when he knew the answer.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped young Omkar?
qa.a: Datta choosing to walk home with him and not mention the shorts; a quiet friend made the difference more than new clothes.

qa.q: How might Datta have felt after laughing with the class?
qa.a: Datta may have felt guilty for joining in, which could be why Datta later walked home beside Omkar in silence.

grounding: An elder recalls being laughed at for older, patched clothes as a boy and how he shrank and hid, learning that difference carries a price.

passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof, so lunch was inside the classroom instead of under the neem tree. Forty tiffins opened at once in the damp air.
Zeenat lifted the lid on her ammi's dried-fish rice. The smell spread fast. Aadhya pinched her nose. “Eww, who brought fish?” Three boys at the back made gagging sounds and pointed.
Zeenat snapped the lid shut. She ate two biscuits from her bag instead and said she wasn't hungry.
The next morning she told Ammi she wanted bread and jam, like everyone else. Ammi looked at her for a long moment and packed it. Zeenat carried the tiffin to school feeling lighter and emptier at the same time.

qa.q: Why was lunch inside the classroom?
qa.a: Rain hammered the tin roof, so lunch was inside instead of under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she carried the bread-and-jam tiffin?
qa.a: She felt mixed: lighter because no one would tease her, but empty and a bit sad at giving up her ammi's food.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond to the teasing at lunch?
qa.a: The teacher could stop the gagging at once, say that every home cooks differently, and make sure Zeenat can eat her lunch in peace.

qa.q: What might Ammi be thinking when she looked at Zeenat for a long moment?
qa.a: Ammi probably guessed something had happened at school and felt sad, but chose to pack the bread and wait for Zeenat to tell her.

grounding: Shows a child laughed at for her homemade tiffin who then copies the group's food, learning early that difference carries a price.

passage: In his first week at the Mumbai school, Jeevan opened his steel tiffin at lunch: puttu and kadala curry, packed by his grandmother. Sachin wrinkled his nose. 'What's that, sawdust?' The whole table laughed. When Jeevan answered a question in class, a few boys copied his accent. By Friday, Jeevan was eating lunch in the corridor. On Monday he asked his mother to pack bread and jam, 'like everyone else'. She looked at him for a long moment. Jeevan didn't say why. He just stared at the puttu mould on the kitchen shelf, feeling angry and small at the same time.

qa.q: What was in Jeevan's tiffin?
qa.a: Puttu and kadala curry, packed by his grandmother.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he stared at the puttu mould?
qa.a: Angry and small at the same time, hurt by the teasing and resentful of having to change.

qa.q: What could Jeevan's mother do after his request?
qa.a: Gently ask what happened at school, and let his teacher know about the teasing so it can be stopped.

qa.q: How might Sachin see his 'sawdust' joke?
qa.a: As just a funny line that made the table laugh, not noticing it pushed Jeevan into the corridor.

grounding: A child laughed at for his homemade tiffin and accent shrinks and tries to copy the group, quietly resentful.
